### Most Famous U.S. Composers – A Quick‑Reference Guide  

| Era / Genre | Composer(s) | Why they’re iconic |
|-------------|--------------|--------------------|
| **Early 20th Century** | **George Gershwin** (1898–1937) | Blended jazz idioms into Broadway hits (“Rhapsody in Blue,” “I Got Rhythm”) and created one of America’s first symphonic jazz pieces. |
| | **Aaron Copland** (1900–1990) | His lush orchestration captured the open‑space feel of the American West—think *Appalachian Spring* and *Fanfare for the Common Man*. |
| | **Charles Ives** (1874–1954) | Pioneered experimental techniques while still rooted in folk tunes; his *Concord Sonata* remains a staple of modern repertoire. |
| **Mid‑century Pop & Show Tunes** | **Leonard Bernstein** (1918–1990) | Scored *West Side Story*, *On the Town*, and taught millions through PBS’s *Great Performances*. |
| | **Cole Porter** (1891–1964) | Master lyricist/composer whose songs (*Night and Day*, *Anything Goes*) became standards worldwide. |
| **Film Scores** | **John Williams** (b. 1942) | Legendary Hollywood composer behind *Star Wars*, *Jaws*, *Indiana Jones*, *Harry Potter* series—his themes dominate pop culture. |
| | **Ennio Morricone** (1928–2020) | Though Italian, he spent decades scoring films in the U.S.; his work on *Once Upon a Time…in the West* and *The Good, the Bad and the Ugly* shaped Western soundtracks globally. |
| **Contemporary Minimalists** | **Philip Glass** (b. 1937) | Co‑founder of minimalism; prolific output includes operas (*Einstein on the Beach*), concertos, and film scores. |
| | **Steve Reich** (b. 1936) | Known for phasing patterns and repetitive structures; seminal works include *Music for 18 Musicians* and *Different Trains*. |
| **Jazz & Blues Influences** | **Scott Joplin** (1868–1917) | King of ragtime; *Maple Leaf Rag* remains emblematic of early African‑American popular music. |
| | **Duke Ellington** (1899–1974) | Prolific bandleader and composer who elevated big‑band jazz to art form status. |
| **Modern Orchestral Voices** | **William Grant Still** (1895–1987) | First Black composer to have a full-length opera performed at Carnegie Hall; known as the “Dean” of African‑American musicians. |
| | **Samuel Barber** (1910–2001) | Best remembered for *Adagio for Strings* and *Knoxville: Summer of 1915*, which remain staples of the concert hall. |

#### How These Names Were Chosen  
- **Historical Impact:** Their works helped define genres (e.g., Gershwin’s jazz‑orchestra fusion).  
- **Cultural Reach:** Themes from their compositions appear in movies, TV shows, commercials, and everyday life.  
- **Critical Acclaim:** Multiple awards (Grammy, Pulitzer, Academy Awards) and enduring performance frequency.  
- **Educational Influence:** Many were teachers or mentors shaping generations of musicians (Bernstein, Copland).

---

> **Quick Tip:** If you’re looking for a specific genre (classical, jazz, film score, etc.), narrow down your search within this table—it’ll help pinpoint the right composer for whatever project or listening session you have planned!
